summary: Describes an optional IS-IS mechanism for running several independent IP topologies inside a single IS-IS domain. It can be used for things like a separate management network over the original one. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: One road network can have several separate sets of roads on top, such as one set for buses only. This lets a router network do something like it.

subtitle: Run several independent IP topologies inside one IS-IS routing domain, each with its own shortest-path tree.

tldr.problem: A standard IS-IS domain has one topology, so every route follows the same paths. Operators sometimes want a separate management network, separate IPv6 or multicast paths, or a subset of addresses on different paths.
tldr.mechanism: Routers tag adjacencies, neighbor advertisements and prefixes with a Multi-Topology ID carried in new TLVs. Each topology runs its own SPF computation, and the standard topology is MT ID 0.
tldr.outcome: One IS-IS domain can carry several independent topologies at once, while routers that do not understand the extension keep working with the standard topology.

today: RFC 5120 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multiple Topologies
sections.content:
RFC 5120 describes an optional extension to IS-IS, the routing protocol many ISPs use inside their networks. It lets a single IS-IS domain run a set of independent IP topologies, called Multi-Topologies (MTs).

The RFC lists several uses: an in-band management network on top of the original topology, separate routing domains for isolated multicast or IPv6 islands inside the backbone, or forcing a subset of an address space to follow a different topology. To keep the text simple, the standard IS-IS topology is defined to be MT ID 0.

The work is split into forming adjacencies, advertising neighbors and prefixes per topology, and then running a topology-aware SPF computation.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a network wants more than one map at once, like a normal map and a map just for the repair crew. This RFC explains how routers can keep several maps in one network.

sections.title: Adjacencies and Neighbor Advertisements
sections.content:
Each adjacency MUST be classified as belonging to a set of MTs on the interface. A new TLV in the IS-IS Hello (IIH) packet says which topologies the interface belongs to. If MT 0 is the only topology, the TLV is optional, and leaving it out means MT 0 only.

On a point-to-point link, adjacencies form as usual. A router MUST NOT include a neighbor in its LSPs for a topology if that topology is missing from the neighbor's hellos, and SHOULD NOT form an adjacency if there is no common MT on the interface.

On a LAN, two routers SHALL always establish an adjacency, even with no common MT, so that all routers elect the same Designated Intermediate System (DIS). The pseudo-node LSP built by the DIS is unchanged and lists every node on the LAN regardless of MT capability, because a DIS that does not understand MT cannot be prevented from generating it. A router includes the MT Intermediate Systems TLV for a topology only for neighbors in that topology, and only if it takes part in the topology itself.
sections.eli5: Routers tell their neighbors which maps they use. Two neighbors only share a map if both of them know it, but on a shared hallway everyone still has to talk so they can pick the same leader.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
Four new TLVs carry the topology information. The RFC chose new TLVs instead of sub-TLVs in the existing type-22 and type-135 TLVs because topologies are often not congruent, so sub-TLVs would not save LSP space, because type 22 already has many sub-TLVs and a size limit, and because later per-topology features can inherit the standard attributes.

  • Multi-Topology TLV (229): sent in IIHs and LSP fragment zero. It holds 2-byte entries with an overload bit (O), an attach bit (A), reserved bits and a 12-bit MT ID. It can advertise up to 127 MTs, and a router that sends it MUST list every MT it joins, including ID 0.
  • MT Intermediate Systems TLV (222): a 2-byte MT field followed by the extended IS reachability format of type 22. It is ignored if the MT ID is zero.
  • MT Reachable IPv4 Prefixes TLV (235): a 2-byte MT field followed by the extended IP reachability format of type 135. It is ignored if the MT ID is zero.
  • MT Reachable IPv6 Prefixes TLV (237): a 2-byte MT field followed by the IPv6 reachability format of type 236.

Reserved bits SHOULD be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt. The overload and attach bits in the MT TLV are only valid in LSP fragment zero for MTs other than ID 0.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds four new kinds of labels to the messages routers send. Each label says which map a piece of information belongs to.

sections.title: Per-Topology SPF and Special Bits
sections.content:
Each MT MUST run its own instance of the decision process. The pseudo-node LSPs are shared by all topologies during computation, and the reverse-connectivity check inside SPF MUST follow the same MT so reachability is bidirectional within that topology.

Results SHOULD normally be stored in a separate RIB per topology, since overlapping addresses in different topologies could otherwise cause undesirable routing such as forwarding loops. The next hops derived from an MT's SPF MUST belong to adjacencies of the same MT. The RFC does not let one topology calculate routes from another topology's information inside SPF.

The overload, partition and attached bits in the LSP header only reflect the default topology. MT does not support MT-based partition repair, but each non-default topology can set its own attach and overload bits in the MT TLV. Route leaking between levels SHOULD only happen within the same MT.
sections.eli5: Each map gets its own shortest-path planning, and the answers are kept in separate notebooks. A bus route is never planned using the walking-path notebook.

sections.title: Reserved MT ID Values
sections.content:
Some MT IDs are assigned a fixed purpose. The RFC splits the 12-bit ID space this way:

  • 0: the standard topology.
  • 1: IPv4 in-band management.
  • 2: IPv6 routing topology.
  • 3: IPv4 multicast routing topology.
  • 4: IPv6 multicast routing topology.
  • 5: IPv6 in-band management.
  • 6 to 3995: reserved for IETF consensus.
  • 3996 to 4095: development, experimental and proprietary features.
sections.eli5: Some map numbers are saved for special jobs, like number 1 for the repair crew. Others are free for people to try out their own ideas.

sections.title: Forwarding and Management Considerations
sections.content:
Using MT can leave a system with several RIBs, so packets must be matched to the right one. If each MT is a different address family, such as IPv4 and IPv6, they can share an interface and the address family picks the RIB. If MTs of one family have dedicated interfaces, each interface maps to its own RIB and FIB. If several MTs share an interface and their addresses overlap, an extra mechanism is needed, for example the DSCP bits or the source address, and the RFC calls this a local policy and configuration decision that is outside its scope. If addresses do not overlap, routes from different MTs can be installed in a shared RIB.

An MT may also be used even when its RIB is not used for forwarding, such as for a multicast RPF check, but an incoming packet MUST still be identified as belonging to one topology.

For management, an operator can build a dedicated management topology that includes all nodes, optionally installing its routes in the default RIB when addresses do not overlap. Alternatively the default topology can be extended to all nodes, in which case operators SHOULD set high costs on the extended links so ordinary data traffic is not forwarded through them.
sections.eli5: When a car arrives at a crossroads, the router has to decide which map to use for it. The RFC gives a few ways to decide but leaves the choice to each network.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
IS-IS security applies, and the RFC says no specific security issues are known. Authentication of IS-IS PDUs is the same regardless of MT information. An authentication mechanism such as the one in RFC 3567 SHOULD be applied if modification of multi-topology information is a high risk.

When topologies share an interface in the same address space, something beyond IS-IS must choose the right forwarding table. A misconfiguration or a spoofed source address can lead to packet loss or unauthorized use of premium network resources.

IANA reflected the four new TLV types (222, 229, 235 and 237) in the IS-IS TLV registry and created the registry "IS-IS Multi-Topology Parameters". MT IDs 6 to 3995 are allocated through Expert Review, and 3996 to 4095 are for Private Use.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change the maps could cause trouble, so the RFC suggests locking the messages with a password-like check. It also says to be careful that each car uses the right map.
